text:
Newfoundland Supreme Court

Court of Appeal

Citation: R. v. Brown

Date: 1991-07-29

Docket: 1989 No. 15

Between:

R. (Appellant)

and

Allan G. Brown (Respondent)

Goodridgc, C.J.N., Mahoney and Steele, JJ.A.

Counsel:

Colin Flynn, for the appellant Crown;

No appearance for the respondent accused.

[
1
]

Steele, J.A.: The Crown requests leave to appeal and, if granted,
appeals a decision [See
1989 CanLII 4858 (NL SC)
, 73 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 350; 229 A.P.R. 350.] of Mr.
Justice Kevin Barry of the Trial Division of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland
sitting as a summary conviction appeal court (s. 812(g)) of the
Criminal
Code,
R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, on an appeal from a summary jurisdiction court
(
ss. 785
and
798
) concerning an information alleging an offence contrary to the

Wild Life Act,
Chapter 400, Revised Statutes of Newfoundland 1970
(sometimes called the
Act
). The appeal to this court is taken on a
ground that involves a question of law alone (s. 839), namely, whether s. 12 of
the
Wild Life Act
infringes s. 15(1) (equality rights) of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms

(the
Charter
).

The respondent
complains that arbitrary seizure of his gun by a wild life officer for alleged
breach of a regulation with automatic forfeiture upon conviction - no
discretion in the judge -results in unequal and discriminatory treatment.

[
2
]

Section 17 of the
Act
states in part that offences under
the
Act
or
Regulations
are triable summarily before a Provincial Court judge. Part I of the
Summary Proceedings Act,
S.N. 1979, c. 35,
provides for the enforcement of any penalty or imprisonment prescribed by a
provincial statute on summary conviction before a Provincial Court judge and s.
7 adopts the provisions of the
Criminal Code

respecting summary
convictions and its proceedings.

Chronology

[
3
]

In October of 1987 R.C.M.P. Constable Anthony Pittman was
checking motor vehicles on the Trans Canada Highway, Gander, Newfoundland, for
seat belt regulation violations. He stopped the respondent, Allan Brown. During
the conversation with Brown concerning his driver’s licence and vehicle
registration, Constable Pittman observed a rifle bolt and a partially loaded
ammunition magazine in the glove compartment of the vehicle. Looking to the
rear of the driver’s seat the Constable saw a barrel of a .303 rifle that was
clearly visible under some helmets and a coat. The rifle was not wrapped and
tied and it was not cased, though the R.C.M.P. Constable saw a rifle case
beneath it. The respondent was in possession of a big game hunting licence for
Moose Management Area 24 but the area in which he was travelling and stopped
was Area 23, a closed area. Constable Pittman seized the rifle.

[
4
]

On October 21st, 1987, Constable Pittman laid an information
charging that Brown:

“On or about the 9th day of October 1987, at or near Gander,
in the Province of Newfoundland, being the holder of a game licence and
travelling to a hunting area, did unlawfully transport a firearm during the
closed season in an area known to be frequented by wild life while the firearm
was not cased or securely wrapped or tied, in violation of section 82(1) of the

Wild Life Regulations,
1984, thereby committing an offence contrary to
section 18 of the
Wild Life Act,
Chapter 400, of the Revised Statutes of
Newfoundland, 1979.”

[
5
]

Section 82(1) of the
Wild Life Regulations,
1984, reads as
follows:

“No person other than a person holding a permit to carry,
transport or possess firearms or ammunition issued to him by the Minister or
his agent, shall during the closed season, carry, transport or possess any
firearm or ammunition, in any place known to be frequented by wild life; but a
person travelling to a hunting area may, if he holds the proper game licence, carry,
transport or possess a firearm or ammunition in an area known to be frequented
by wild life if the firearm is cased or securely wrapped and tied.”

[
6
]

Section 18 of the
Act
states that every person who
contravenes or fails to comply with the
Act
or the
Regulations
is
guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction, where no other penalty
is specified, to a fine not exceeding $500. The summary conviction court
convicted the respondent of a breach of s. 82(1) of the
Regulations
as
specified in the information. He was fined $100 but the trial judge refused to
declare or confirm that the rifle seized by Constable Pittman was forfeited pursuant
to s. 12 of the
Wild Life Act
as amended in 1985.

[
7
]

Section 12 of the
Wild Life Act
provides as follows:

“12 A wild life officer may, without a warrant, enter and
search any

a) logging camp, mining camp or construction camp,

b) trapping camp, hunting camp, fishing camp or other camp,

c) summer cottage or other structure erected in an area
frequented by wild life, and

d) any vehicle or near an area frequented by wild life,

in which he has reasonable cause to suspect any gun or other
firearm is being kept or had contrary to this Act or the regulations and may,
on view, seize the gun or other firearm,
and upon conviction
of any
person in respect thereof
the gun or other firearm is, in addition to any
other punishment imposed, forfeited
to Her Majesty in right of Newfoundland
and may be disposed of as the Minister directs.” (my emphasis added)

Upon conviction the sentencing judge has no discretion
respecting forfeiture of a seized firearm: it is mandatory. It results from and
accompanies the conviction.

[
8
]

The charge before the summary conviction court was an alleged
violation of the
Wild Life Regulations.
The respondent was convicted and
fined and from that determination there is no complaint. Forfeiture occurs upon
conviction by virtue of the legislation without judicial intervention. There is
doubt in my mind therefore whether the summary conviction court on the
information before it had jurisdiction to challenge the seizure and forfeiture
provisions and to declare s. 12 of the
Act
unconstitutional. However, as
the summary conviction court and the summary conviction appeal court proceeded
on the assumption of jurisdiction in the lower court and the Crown on this
appeal has not raised the matter of jurisdiction, I will not address the issue.

Disposition In Courts Below

[
9
]

In repudiating and purportedly nullifying the seizure and
forfeiture provisions of s. 12 of the
Act,
the summary conviction court
invoked s. 15(1) (equality rights) of the
Charter
:

“Every individual is equal before and under the law and has
the right to the equal protection and equal benefit of the law without
discrimination and, in particular, without discrimination based on race,
national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability.”

[
10
]

The Crown appealed the ruling of the summary conviction court
only in respect to the unconstitutionality of s. 12 of the
Wild Life Act.

[
11
]

The summary conviction appeal judge found that the trial judge
was not in error in refusing to order or confirm forfeiture of the respondent’s
firearm and in finding the seizure and forefeiture provisions of s. 12 of the
Act

invalid. He ordered the gun be returned to the respondent. In dismissing
the Crown’s appeal, Justice Barry relied on the reasons he gave in an earlier
decision,
R. v. Hillyard
(1988),
1988 CanLII 5421 (NL SC)
, 72 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 334; 223 A.P.R.
334 (Nfld. S.C.T.D.). The facts of that case are different only in the section
of the
Regulations
breached, that is to say, s. 82(17) prohibiting the
carrying, transport or possession of a loaded firearm in a motor vehicle. The
gun was seized but the summary conviction court decided that the seizure and
forfeiture provisions of s. 12 of the
Act
were contrary to
ss. 7
,
8
,
12

and
15
of the
Charter
.
Only s. 15 of the
Charter
was analyzed and
applied.

[
12
]

In
Hillyard

the appeal court judge found that Hillyard’s
equality rights under
s. 15
of the
Charter

were violated by the seizure
and forfeiture provisions of s. 12 of the
Act.
He concluded that the
section was unfair and discriminatory to those affected by its seizure and forfeiture
provisions. The appeal judge next considered
s. 1
of the
Charter
and
concluded (1) that the infringement of Hillyard’s equality rights under s.
15(1) was not a reasonable limit prescribed by law which can be demonstrably
justified in a free and democratic society within the meaning of s. 1 of the
Charter;

and (2) that the requirement of mandatory forfeiture of firearms seized at
the instance of a wild life officer was not redeemed under s. 1 of the
Charter.

[
13
]

Justice Barry found that the application of s. 12 of the
Act
authorizing
seizure and forfeiture of a gun where it was suspected that it was kept or had
contrary to the
Act
or
Regulations,
gave rise to unfair and
unequal treatment. He concluded, and I take the liberty of paraphrasing him,
that:

(1) guns seized by wild life officers pursuant to s. 12 of the

Act
are automatically forfeited on conviction, meaning that wild life
officers in the exercise of their discretion to seize, arbitrarily
differentiate between similarly placed persons;

(2) guns vary greatly in value and those who own a gun of
great value and have it seized and forfeited on conviction are penalized
disproportionally compared to an owner having a gun of little value forfeited;

(3) s. 11 of the
Act
in certain circumstances permits
seizure of “implements” common to hunters that includes guns and firearms;
forfeiture is a discretionary power vested in the trial judge and unlike the
automatic forfeiture provision of s. 12; this means that on seizure pursuant to
s. 11, say for example a serious breach of the Act or Regulations, a hunter may
not lose his gun by forfeiture but a hunter having his gun seized under s. 12
for a minor breach would on conviction, ipso facto, lose his gun by forfeiture;
and,

(4) upon a s. 11 seizure where the person in possession at the
time of seizure is not the owner, the owner has an opportunity to prove
ownership and have his firearm returned; not so an owner on a s. 12 seizure.

[
14
]

For these reasons the summary conviction appeal court judge
upheld the ruling of the summary conviction court refusing to order or confirm
forfeiture of the respondent’s gun. He held that s. 12 of the Wild Life Act was
unconstitutional for the reasons given in Hillyard.

Issue

[
15
]

The question posed on this appeal is whether s. 12 of the
Wild
Life Act,
R.S.N. 1970, c. 400, is contrary to
s. 15
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, Constitution Act, 1982.

Supreme Court: Unravelling Section 15(1)

[
16
]

It is right that I immediately point out that the appeal court
judge in late 1988 and January 1989, when he filed his decision, did not have
the benefit of reading three relatively recent judgments of the Supreme Court
of Canada that for the first time perceptively examine and elucidate the
equality rights as described in
s. 15
of the
Charter
. I suspect that most legal
writing to date touching
s. 15
will have to be reconsidered. These three cases,

Andrews v. Law Society of British Columbia,

1989 CanLII 2 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 143; 91 N.R.
255; [1989] 2 W.W.R. 289; 56 D.L.R.(4th) 1;
Reference Re Workers’ Compensation
Act (Nfld.),

1989 CanLII 86 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 922; 96 N.R. 227; 76 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 181;
235 A.P.R. 181; 56 D.L.R.(4th) 765; and
R. v. Turpin,

1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
, [1989] 1 S.C.R.
1296; 96 N.R. 115; 34 O.A.C. 115; 48 C.C.C.(3d) 8; 69 C.R.(3d) 97, confront
s.
15
in a manner that was not generally foreseen or contemplated. I trust I will
be forgiven for saying therefore that not much is to be gained by studying the
reasons for judgment of the appeal judge written prior to these three
decisions. Nevertheless, his conclusions and indeed the complaints of the
respondent of unequal and discriminatory treatment raise serious questions that
must be resolved but in the light of current thinking about
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter.

Andrews v. Law Society of B.C.

[
17
]

Andrews involved an individual who was a permanent resident of Canada who met all requirements for admission to the British Columbia Bar except for
citizenship, a requirement under the
Barristers and Solicitors Act
for
admission into the legal profession. His action for a declaration that that
requirement violates s. 15(1) was dismissed at trial but allowed on appeal. The
Supreme Court of Canada dismissed the appeal, holding that the citizenship
requirement contravened
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter

and is not justified
under
s. 1
. The majority judgment was delivered by Wilson, J., with Dickson,
C.J.C., and L’Heureux-Dube, J., concurring. The dissenting judgment was by
McIntyre, J., with Lamer, J., concurring. LaForest, J., concurred with the
majority. It is important to note that Justice Wilson expressed complete
agreement with Justice McIntyre on the way in which s. 15(1) of the
Charter

should be interpreted and applied and as to the way in which s. 15(1) and
s. 1

of the Charter interact. The disagreement between the majority and the minority
was solely on the application of
s. 1
to the particular facts. As we shall see
much of the helpful commentary on s. 15(1) is to be found in the writing of
McIntyre, J., in
Andrews
and Wilson, J., in
Turpin
.

[
18
]

Justice McIntyre discusses the concept of equality in s. 15(1)
and sees the rights as a guarantee of equality before and under the law as well
as the equal protection and benefit of the law without discrimination. However,
he comments at pp. 163-164 S.C.R.: “This is not a general guarantee of
equality; it does not provide for equality between individuals or groups within
society in a general or abstract sense, nor does it impose on individuals or
groups an obligation to accord equal treatment to others. It is concerned with
the application of the law.”

[
19
]

McLachlin, J.A., (as she then was) in the British Columbia Court
of Appeal in
Andrews,
1986 CanLII 1287 (BC CA)
, 27 D.L.R.(4d) 600, at p. 605, expressed the
opinion that:

“... the essential meaning of the constitutional requirement
of equal protection and equal benefit is that persons who are ‘similarly
situated be similarly treated’ and conversely, that persons who are
‘differently situated be differently treated’ ...”

In
Andrews
Mclntyre, J., refers to the above statement by
McLachlin, J.A., and goes on to say that in applying this test she was adopting
a proposition widely accepted, with some modification, by courts throughout Canada. He points out that the “similarly situated test” was a restatement of the
Aristotelian Principle of formal equality. Nevertheless, he considers the test
as seriously flawed because it excluded consideration of the nature of the law.
At p. 167 S.C.R.:

“... mere equality of application to similarly situated groups
or individuals does not afford a realistic test for violation of equality
rights. For, as had been said, a bad law will not be saved merely because it
operates equally upon those to whom it has application. Nor will a law
necesssarily be bad because it makes distinctions.”.

And at pp. 168-169 S.C.R.:

“For the reasons outlined above, the test cannot be accepted
as a fixed rule or formula for the resolution of equality questions arising
under the
Charter
.
Consideration must be given to the content of the
law, to its purpose, and its impact upon those to whom it applies, and also
upon those whom it excludes from its application. The issues which will arise
from case to case are such that it would be wrong to attempt to confine these
considerations within such a fixed and limited formula.

“It is not every distinction or differentiation in treatment
at law which will transgress the equality guarantees of
s. 15
of the
Charter
.

It is, of course, obvious that legislatures may - and to govern effectively
- must treat different individuals and groups in different ways. Indeed, such
distinctions are one of the main preoccupations of legislatures. The
classifying of individuals and groups, the making of different provisions
respecting such groups, the application of different rules, regulations,
requirements and qualifications to different persons is necessary for the
governance of modern society. As noted above, for the accommodation of
differences, which is the essence of true equality, it will frequently be
necessary to make distinctions. What kinds of distinctions will be acceptable
under s. 15(1) and what kinds will violate its provisions?”

[
20
]

I have considered so far the concept of equality, but s. 15 has,
in a sense, a limitation or qualifier, namely, that the equality rights be
without discrimination. The notion of discrimination adds a new dimension and
particularly so where the personal characteristics of the individual or group
are expressly enumerated and destined to be directive. The enumerated grounds
reflect the most common root of discrimination giving rise to infringement of
the equality rights; they establish the general framework by indicating the
scope and orientation of the section.

[
21
]

At p. 174 of
Andrews
Justice McIntyre proposes the
following definition of discrimination:

“... I would say then that discrimination may be described as
a distinction, whether intentional or not but based on grounds relating to
personal characteristics of the individual or group, which has the effect of
imposing burdens, obligations, or disadvantages ort such individual or group
not imposed upon others, or which withholds or limits access to opportunities,
benefits, and advantages available to other members of society.”

[
22
]

In defining discrimination McIntyre, J., favoured the “enumerated
and analogous grounds” approach. At p. 182 of
Andrews
he says:

“The third or ‘enumerated and analogous grounds’ approach most
closely accords with the purposes of s. 15 and the definition of discrimination
outlined above and leaves questions of justification to s. 1. However, in
assessing whether a complainant’s rights have been infringed under s. 15(1), it
is not enough to focus only on the alleged ground of discrimination and decide
whether or not it is an enumerated or analogous ground. The effect of the
impugned distinction or classification on the complainant must be considered.
Once it is accepted that not all distinctions and differentiations created by
law are discriminatory, then a role must be assigned to s. 15(1) which goes
beyond the mere recognition of a legal distinction.”

[
23
]

In accepting the enumerated and analogous grounds approach in
Andrews

the court decidedly narrowed the application of s. 15(1). Its scope is
restricted to the enumerated and the unenumerated but analogous grounds of s.
15(1). If there was ever doubt about this result, it was dissolved by the
Workers’
Compensation Reference.

Workers’ Compensation Reference

[
24
]

This case was heard by the Supreme Court of Canada on the heals
of
Andrews
and a matter of weeks before
Turpin.
The judgment of
the court was delivered orally by La Forest, J., and is comprised of a single
paragraph. The case involved the right to compensation provided by the
Workers’
Compensation Act
in lieu of all rights and actions to which a worker or
dependents might otherwise be entitled. The issue was whether the statutory
right to compensation that precluded any other action was discriminatory. The
judgment states in part at p. 924:

“The situation of the workers and dependents here is in no way
analogous to those listed in s. 15(1), as a majority in
Andrews
stated
was required to permit recourse to s. 15(1).”

The import of this brief statement is to confirm the court’s
resolve expressed in
Andrews
that the scope of the equality rights in s.
15(1) be greatly confined. The success of this design rests on the definition
of discrimination and more precisely the acceptance of the means or expedient
to determine the personal characteristics of an individual or group considered
to be analogous to those enumerated in s. 15(1).

R. v. Turpin

[
25
]

Turpin,
the third of the three recent decisions of the
Supreme Court, applies
Andrews
and the judgment of the court by Wilson,
J., amplifies the construction of s. 15(1). The facts in
Turpin

(borrowing
from the headnote - (1989),
1989 CanLII 98 (SCC)
, 48 C.C.C.(3d) 8) are that the accused were charged
in Ontario with first degree murder and at the commencement of the trial were
permitted by the trial judge to elect to be tried by judge alone. At the time,
the
Criminal Code

required that an accused charged with murder be tried
by a superior court judge and jury except in Alberta where, pursuant to
s. 430

of the
Criminal Code,
the accused, with the consent of the trial judge,
could elect trial by judge alone. The trial judge in this case however, held
that the accused were entitled to elect trial by judge alone by virtue of
s.
11(f)
of the
Charter
.

[
26
]

In
Turpin

the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, holding
that the accuseds’ equality rights were not infringed because accused persons
in their position in Alberta had by law (
Criminal Code
) an opportunity
to be tried by judge alone. The court held that the accused were denied equality
before the law but there could only be a violation of
s. 15
if the infringement
of the right to equality before the law results in discrimination and there was
no discrimination. It could not be said that persons resident outside Alberta and charged with s. 427 offences are members of a “discrete and insular minority”.
They repudiated the idea that it is a fundamental principle under
s. 15
that
the criminal law apply equally throughout the country.

[
27
]

Justice Wilson in
Turpin

at pp. 13311332 comments on “the
enumerated and analogous grounds” approach and a “discrete and insular
minority” coming within the ambit of
s. 15
:

“In determining whether there is discrimination on grounds
relating to the personal characteristics of the individual or group, it is important
to look not only at the impugned legislation which has created a distinction
that violates the right to equality but also the larger social, political and
legal context McIntyre, J., emphasized in
Andrews
[at p. 12 D.L.R.]:
‘For as has been said, a bad law will not be saved merely because it operates
equally upon those to whom it has application. Nor will a law necessarily be
bad because it makes distinctions.’ Accordingly, it is only by examining the
larger context that a court can determine whether differential treatment
results in inequality or whether, contrariwise, it would be identical treatment
which would in the particular context result in inequality or foster
disadvantage. A finding that there is discrimination will, I think, in most but
perhaps not all cases, necessarily entail a search for disadvantage that exists
apart from and independent of the particular legal distinction being
challenged.

“McIntyre, J., recognized in
Andrews
that ‘the
“enumerated and analogous grounds” approach most closely accords with the
purposes of
s. 15
and the definition of discrimination outlined above’ and
suggested that the alleged victims of discrimination in
Andrews,
i.e,
noncitizens permanently resident in Canada were ‘a good example of a “discrete
and insular minority” who came within the protection of
s. 15
’. Similarly, I
suggested in my reasons in
Andrews
that the determination of whether a
group falls into an analogous category to those specifically enumerated in
s.
15
is ‘not to be made only in the context of the law which is subject to
challenge but rather in the context of the place of the group in the entire
social, political and legal fabric of our society’. If the larger context is
not examined, the
s. 15
analysis may become a mechanical and sterile categorization
process conducted entirely within the four corners of the impugned legislation.
A determination as to whether or not discrimination is taking place, if based
exclusively on an analysis of the law under challenge is likely, in my view, to
result in the same kind of circularity which characterized the similarly
situated similarly treated text clearly rejected by this court in
Andrews.
”

The Supreme Court in
Turpin

endeavours to further clarify
the meaning of discrimination and in doing so struggles to find a useful
definition of the phrase “discrete and insular minority”. It is apparent that
Workers’
Compensation Reference
and
Turpin
advance the premise emerging from
Andrews

that only the enumerated and unen-umerated grounds that can be said to be
analogous to the enumerated grounds can fall within the equality rights
protected by s. 15(1).

Section 15: Supreme Court’s Analysis

[
28
]

It is evident that the equality rights described in
s. 15
that
every individual is equal before and under the law and has the right to the
equal protection and benefit of the law is a notion distinguishable from the
conceptualization of discrimination. The expectation implicit in the equality
rights is that all persons will be subject to the equal demands and burdens of
the law with equal protection and benefit knowing that they will not be subject
to any greater disadvantage or penalty by operation or application of the law.
The guarantee of equality rights in s. 15(1) has a proviso, namely, that
equality in law be “without discrimination”. If a law by its application or
impact provokes different treatment or distinctions with discrimination, there
is a violation of s. 15(1). Where discrimination is found, it follows that
there has been an infringement of s. 15(1). What we now see is a nicety: not
every case of difference in treatment by law will breach the equality rights
and not every difference in treatment will give rise to discrimination.

[
29
]

The three recent decisions of the Supreme Court signify that
every difference in treatment between individuals under the law will not
necessarily result in inequality and, for that matter, identical treatment may
well produce inequality. Equality is an ideal but the main consideration must
be the impact of the law on the individual or group affected. Equality of
application to similarly situated groups or individuals may not be the
definitive test for violation of the equality rights, but it cannot be doubted
that the purpose of
s. 15
is to ensure equality in the formation and
application of the law.

[
30
]

McIntyre, J., in
Andrews
defines discrimination as a
distinction based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of the
individual or group and causing burdens, obligations or disadvantages on some
but not imposed upon others or which withholds or limits access to
opportunities, benefits and advantages available to others. Discrimination in
s. 15(1) is limited to discrimination caused by the application or operation of
law. The enumerated grounds of discrimination found in s. 15(1) are not intended
to be absolute, but they do mark the sweep and scope of the section.

[
31
]

Discrimination frequently originates in connection with the
personal characteristics enumerated in s. 15(1). It is not sufficient to make a
finding of a distinction in the treatment of groups or individuals. The other
component to be reckoned with is whether the denial of an equality right, if
that be the case, results in discrimination. Differential treatment is
permitted under
s. 15
provided it is “without discrimination” (McIntyre, J., in

Andrews
at pp. 181-182).

[
32
]

Where there has been an infringement of an equality right and a
finding of discrimination is made, a breach of s. 15(1) is the consequence.
Justification for the infringement of the equality right(s) with discrimination
must then be considered within the context of
s. 1
of the
Charter
.

[
33
]

The court in
Turpin

made it clear that it is not a
fundamental principle under
s. 15
of the
Charter

that the criminal law
be applied equally throughout the country. At p. 1334 of
Turpin,
Wilson,
J., advocates a case-by-case analysis, as occurred in
Andrews,
the
purpose being to determine (1) whether the distinction created by the impugned
legislation results in a violation of one of the equality rights and, if so,
(2) whether that distinction is discriminatory in its purpose or effect.

[
34
]

The Supreme Court discredits the “similarly situated” test. That
test necessitates a decision whether individuals or groups are similarly
situated and, if so, only then to determine if different treatment was proper.
I have already referred to Justice McIntyre’s abrupt dismissal of the similarly
situated test. At p. 166 of
Andrews
he also condemned the test in these
terms:

“The test as stated, however, is seriously deficient in that
it excludes any consideration of the nature of the law. If it were to be
applied literally, it could be used to justify the Nuremberg Laws of Adolf
Hitler. Similar treatment was contemplated for all Jews.”

[
35
]

In
Turpin

Wilson, J., writing for the court affirms the
court’s repudiation of the similarly situated test in
Andrews:
“... the
similarly situated similarly treated test clearly rejected by this court in
Andrews
”
(p. 1332).

[
36
]

There are, however, academics who feel we may not have heard the
last of the “similarly situated” analysis: Dale Gibson,
The Law of the
Charter: Equality Rights
(1990); Mark Gold,
Comment: Andrews v. Law
Society of B.C.
(1989), 34 McGill L.J. 1063, and A. Wayne MacKay and Dianne
Pothier,
Developments in Constitutional Law: The 1988-89 Term
(1990), 1
Supreme Court Law Review (Second Series), page 81. Gibson maintains that
Justice Mclntyre only intended to reject the similarly situated test as a fixed
rule or formula. Gold refers to this test as a case of “... pushing in a bump
on a balloon. It may be flattened, but the bump will reappear at some other
place on the balloon”. MacKay and Pothier take the view that the court did
nonetheless “intend a more general rejection of the ‘similarly situated’ test
as a way of reducing the scope of s. 15 to more manageable limits”. For the
time being the Supreme Court, at the very least, degrades the similarly
situated analysis as a means to assess
s. 15
equality rights.

[
37
]

The three decisions of the Supreme Court leave little doubt that
the court was at pains to narrow the scope of
s. 15
. In his definition of
discrimination in
Andrews,
Justice McIntyre refers to “a distinction ...
based on grounds relating to personal characteristics of the individual or
group The court in the
Workers’ Compensation Reference
is very precise
when it observed that the situation “is in no way analogous to those listed in
s. 15(1), as a majority in
Andrews
stated was required to permit
recourse to s. 15(1)”. Wilson, J., in
Turpin

clearly infers that
distinctions not based on personal characteristics cannot be found to be
discriminating. The court has, therefore, restricted s. 15(1) equality rights
protection to discrimination on the grounds enumerated and to discrimination
based on personal characteristics of the individual or group analogous to the
enumerated grounds. The burden lies on the applicant to establish the personal
characteristic or characteristics analogous to the enumerated grounds. Only
those grounds that are analogous to the enumerated grounds fall within s. 15(1)
and presumably that group is a “discrete and insular minority” - a phrase that
is yet to be satisfactorily defined.

[
38
]

It is with this explanation and construction of s. 15(1) that I
must examine the facts of this case and the assertions of unequal treatment and
discrimination.

Review Of Facts

[
39
]

A very brief review of the facts may be helpful at this point.
Section 82(1) of the
Wild Life Regulation
says in part that a person
holding a game licence and travelling to a hunting area may carry a firearm in
an area frequented by wild life if the firearm is cased or securely wrapped and
tied. Constable Pittman of the R.C.M.P. (a wild life officer) stopped the
respondent Brown on the Trans Canada Highway to check for seat belt violations
and observed a rifle bolt and an ammunition magazine in the glove compartment
and an uncased and unwrapped .303 rifle in the rear of the vehicle. In the
exercise of his discretion he seized the rifle and subsequently laid an
information charging Brown with a breach of the section. A conviction was
recorded in the summary conviction court but the trial judge refused to ratify
forfeiture, holding that s. 12 of the
Act,
which made forfeiture
automatic upon conviction, was unconstitutional. That ruling was upheld on
appeal to the Trial Division of the Supreme Court (Appeal Court) on the ground
that s. 12 was contrary to
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter

and not redeemed
under
s. 1
.

[
40
]

Barry, J., agreed with the summary conviction court that
application of s. 12 -seizure and forfeiture - resulted in unequal treatment
for those in the category he defined as hunters who had firearms seized. I
again paraphrase the complaints: (1) Wild Life Officers arbitrarily decide when
to seize rifles knowingly prescribing forfeiture and thereby differentiating
between similarly placed persons; (2) rifles vary in value, often greatly,
causing disproportionate financial loss upon forfeiture; (3) under s. 11 of the

Act
discretion to order forfeiture is vested in the judge making it
possible for a hunter convicted of a serious breach of the
Act
or
Regulations

not to suffer forfeiture of his seized rifle, whereas a hunter convicted of
a minor offence under s. 12, whose gun is seized, loses it irretrievably; and,
(4) if the person in possession of a rifle seized pursuant to s. 12 of the
Act

is not the owner, upon conviction the rifle is forfeited without recourse
or remedy for the owner. This is quite unlike a seizure under s. 11 of the
Act,

where the owner has an opportunity to prove ownership and have it returned.
For these four reasons the respondent contends that s. 12 of the
Act,
in
its application, leads to unequal treatment and discrimination constituting an
infringement of his equality rights under
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
.

[
41
]

Section 12 of the
Act
is clear that if a wild life officer
has reasonable cause to suspect that a firearm is being kept or had contrary to
the
Act
or
Regulations,
he may upon viewing it - in the exercise
of his judgment - seize it. He seizes the firearm knowing that if the alleged
offender is convicted of the offence the firearm is thereby forfeited. There
are no provisions in the
Act
or
Regulations
establishing
guidelines for seizure of firearms and I do not know the policy or practice, if
one exists, of wild life officers respecting seizures under this section.

[
42
]

The discretion vested in wild life officers to seize firearms
pursuant to s. 12 of the
Act
may, as we have seen, give rise to
differential treatment of hunters: a hunter may have his firearm seized (and if
convicted, lose it by forfeiture); whereas another person in very similar
circumstances may not have his gun seized. The unpredictability of seizure may
exist as between different wild life officers or for that matter by the same
wild life officer. In any given circumstance it would be difficult to
objectively ascertain the rationale for seizure from one but not another.
Seizure may be founded in good faith by a conscientious, hard working wild life
officer only intent on doing his job to the best of his ability. It is also
possible that seizure may be prompted by whimsical, high-handed or wilful
behaviour. On the other hand, it is conceivable that a decision not to seize a
firearm may be motivated by favouritism or a bias of some sort.

[
43
]

There is little doubt that seizure and forfeiture of firearms
pursuant to s. 12 can give rise to differential treatment: some hunters will
have firearms seized and some will not; because of the difference in gun
values, the loss by one because of forfeiture may be disproportionate to
another; a seizure under s. 12 may have a different result from a seizure under
s. 11; and finally, a seizure under s. 11 provides the opportunity for the
owner of a firearm seized (not the person in possession at the time of seizure)
to reclaim his firearm, there being no such remedy for an owner under a s. 12
seizure.

[
44
]

The
Wild Life Act,
and ss. 11 and 12 in particular,
contain provisions that are discordant, at times obscure, and without question
never easy reading. This is partly due to piecemeal amendments. Having conceded
this complexity, I am still bound to add that the consequence is not
discrimination against any individual or group. It does not follow, logically
or at all, that ailing legislation requiring revision to properly reflect
consistency and sound policy inevitably leads to a discriminatory result. In this
case the
Act
contains very wide discretionary powers, without guidance,
the exercise of which may entail differential treatment that borders on a
transgression of one or more of the equality rights. That can happen, as it did
here, but without discrimination. It is a case of “differential treatment
without discrimination” (see Wilson, J., in
Turpin

p. 1330 and McIntyre,
J., in
Andrews,
p. 182).

[
45
]

Where there is differential treatment or a denial of an equality
right the question is whether the result occurred with discrimination. Wilson,
J., emphasized this proposition in
Turpin

at pp. 1330-1331 quoting
McIntyre, J., in
Andrews:

“Differential treatment is permitted under
s. 15
provided it
is ‘without discrimination’. As Mclntyre, J., stated in
Andrews
(at p.
182):

‘A complainant under s. 15(1) must show not only that he or
she is not receiving equal treatment before and under the law or that the law
has a differential impact on him or her in the protection or benefit accorded
by law but, in addition, must show that the legislative impact of the law is
discriminatory.’

“The internal qualification in s. 15 that the differential
treatment be ‘without discrimination’ is determinative of whether or not there
has been a violation of the section. It is only when one of the four equality
rights has been denied with discrimination that the values protected by
s. 15

are threatened and the court’s legitimate role as the protector of such values
comes into play.”

[
46
]

It is evident that the
Act
and s. 12 in particular makes
no distinction based on grounds relating to any personal characteristics of any
individual or group. Section 82(1) of the
Regulations
is directed at all
persons travelling to a hunting area, who hold a proper game licence, and
travel through an area known to be frequented by wild life: they may carry a
firearm if it is cased or securely wrapped and tied. In short, the regulation
is directed at all would be hunters. Section 12 permits seizure where the
individual’s conduct and the state of affairs offends the
Act
or
Regulations.

Clearly, s. 12 and the regulation makes no distinctions based on race,
national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical
disability. The law as written makes no distinctions whatsoever. In my opinion
it is equally true that the law, (
s.
12 of the
Wild Life Act
and
s. 82(1)) of the
Regulations
in its application, purpose and effect, is
not selective of any individual or group based on any of the enumerated grounds
in s. 15(1) or any analogous grounds.
Andrews
and
Turpin
make it
clear that where there is a distinction - differential treatment - the question
is whether the distinctions are discriminatory on grounds relating to personal
characteristics of the individual or group enumerated in s. 15(1) or any
grounds analogous to those grounds. It cannot be said that a decision to seize
a firearm pursuant to s. 11 or 12, and the consequences that follow, has as its
purpose or result the definition or setting apart of any particular individual,
group or class of persons because of common traits, qualities or quirks that
can reasonably be said to be analogous to the personal characteristics
enumerated in s. 15(1). Admittedly; there is differential treatment but not
distinctions inspired by or resulting in discrimination.

[
47
]

In summary, it is evident that the differential treatment or
unequal treatment, if that be the case, occurs without discrimination against
any particular individual or group. No person, group or category can be
identified on the basis of the enumerated grounds in s. 15(1) or any analogous
grounds. What we have is a statute, not without flaws or shortcomings, that
arguably results in unequal treatment. It is not, however, differential
treatment that is discriminatory because a particular section of the legislation
isolates and unfairly treats individuals or groups on the grounds of personal
characteristics or attributes.

Conclusion:

[
48
]

On appeal to the summary conviction appeal court Justice Barry
agreed that s. 12 of the
Wild Life Act
was contrary to
s. 15
of the
Charter

and he upheld the ruling of the summary conviction court that the seizure
and forfeiture provisions of s. 12 were invalid. It was from that judgment that
the appellant appeals. The issue on this appeal is whether s. 12 of the
Wild
Life Act
is contrary to s. 15 of the
Charter.
For reasons explained
it is not. I conclude that the seizure and forfeiture by the wild life officer
of the respondent’s firearm was not an infringement of the equality rights with
discrimination as described in s. 15 of the
Charter.
For this reason
consideration of
s. 1
of the
Charter,
(justification for an
infringement), does not arise.

[
49
]

Section 12 of the
Act
is explicit in that the wild life
officer may, without a warrant, enter the places mentioned in which he has
reasonable cause to suspect any gun or firearm has been kept or had contrary to
the
Act
or the
Regulations
and on view may seize it. Upon
conviction the gun or firearm is, in addition to any other punishment imposed,
forfeited. Forfeiture of the firearm is complete upon formal entry of the
conviction - it is a fait accompli. Accordingly, no declaration or order by the
trial judge is necessary to perfect forfeiture.

[
50
]

In the ordinary course of events one expects the trial judge to
explain to an accused at the time of his conviction the provisions of the
Act

respecting seizure and forfeiture. It would be prudent upon entering a
conviction to confirm for the record the fact that the firearm is forfeited.

[
51
]

Leave to appeal is granted. The appeal is allowed and the order
of the summary conviction appeal court judge that the respondent’s firearm be
returned is set aside. Appeal allowed.
